| Model probe set 1 (read to write v2, not independent) | 16 / 20 | 25 / 28 |
| Hand set (same author, not independent): exact / U.S. controls clean | 30 / 10 of 10 | 30 / 10 of 10 |

- **Adoption.** All three D681 conditions hold (development 0, held-out 0 ≤ 3, set 2 22 > 19). Production uses `market-detect-v2`. It met the stated expectation of 22 exactly.
- **What it still misses (set 2, read after scoring).** Every miss falls to the United States, and no text was given a wrong non-U.S. market. Four carry a weak hint (a price in JPY, KRW or Canadian dollars; "for sale to Paris hospitals"), so they go to review only if the router says `unclear`. Not read: "importing diagnostic ultrasound probes into France" (three words between verb and "into"; the cue allows two), "Our Osaka distribution network is importing", "ships … to our distribution center in Mexico City", and law names not on the list (Customs Tariff Law, Commerce (Trade Descriptions) Act, "SARS"). About one non-U.S. question in four is still read as U.S. when the caller does not choose the market. Reading: the explicit market choice is the reliable path, so the try-it form and the API take it; the detector is the net under it.
- **Spend.** Probe sets $0.0421 and $0.0398, gateway-reported. Detector runs cost nothing.
- **Commit hashes.** c000fafd, 400f0758, 52410a49 and 5398fa07 in D680 to D682 are the hashes as pushed before each run. The branch was later rebased onto main (twice), which changed the hashes but not the content; find the commits by their subjects ("D680: pre-register…", "Market detector market-detect-v1…", "D681: …", "market-detect-v2 (D681)…"). The pushed times stand.

## D720 — Canada's marking rules as a rules-only table: source, licence, parse (22 Nov, #663)
- **Source:** SOR/94-23, Determination of Country of Origin for the Purpose of Marking Goods (CUSMA Countries) Regulations, as XML from Justice Laws (<https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/XML/SOR-94-23.xml>), retrieved 22 Nov 2026, SHA-256 `ba95f291e6e4d28174e1f27b1d3e7fbda26a45e8058da9a4f2a5573ccd73c44b`. Last amended 1 Jul 2020 (SOR/2020-158), consolidated to 17 Nov 2022. The XML is not committed; `go run ./cmd/tariffshift rules-ca -xml SOR-94-23.xml -retrieved 2026-11-22` rebuilds `backend/internal/tariffshift/rules_ca.json` (version `ca-sor-94-23-v1`).
- **Licence:** the Reproduction of Federal Law Order (SI/97-5, <https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/SI-97-5/FullText.html>, read 22 Nov 2026) lets anyone reproduce federal enactments and their consolidations without charge or permission, if accuracy is kept and the copy is not presented as official. So the row text is committed, with that attribution in the table and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES. CBSA's own rulings are a different licence (written permission for commercial reuse) and are not used.
- **Changes of form:** headings are written `8473` for `84.73` and ranges use a hyphen, so the 19 CFR 102.20 parser reads the rows unchanged. Two slips in the published text are corrected in the table: 59.01-59.11 "with that group" (within), 6815.10-6815.99 "including a subheading" (another subheading).
- **Rows:** 569 code rows, plus a whole-chapter row for chapters 61 and 62 (their only rule sits in the notes row), plus a note-only row for heading 63.09 (its note is its rule; no tariff-shift row exists): 572 rows, 596 "A change ..." alternatives.
- **Parse coverage:** 548 of 596 alternatives encoded (91.9%); 544 rows fully encoded, 4 partly, 24 not at all (including the 63.09 note row). Not encoded, and never decided by code: 40 written by goods description ("a pillow cover of heading 63.04", "any other good of subheading 2208.90", the chapter 61 and 62 rows), 8 with a proviso on content or process (alcohol strength, chemical reaction, direct blending, 60% by weight, electrolytic separation, the yarn rule of 63.08). One parser extension: Canada's "a change to a good of any of subheadings ... from any other good of that subheading or any other heading" (s. 12(2)), read as the codes plus a source in the good's own subheading or heading (D722). The full list prints from `rules-ca`.
- **Notes:** each Schedule III note is matched by its opening words; an unknown note fails the build. Notes that set origin by a process (Section II plants grown, Section VI notes 1 to 3, chapter 27 notes, 63.09 and 63.10) mark their rows (D723).

## D721 — One engine, two rule sets (22 Nov, #663)
- `internal/tariffshift` now takes a rule set: `Table.Regime` names the general rules the rows are applied through (`GeneralRules`: citations, de minimis chapters and measure, and the Canadian steps). Empty is 19 CFR Part 102 as before. The U.S. answers are byte for byte what they were: every committed `-check` (eval, parts-example, plans-example, plans102-example) passes unchanged, and `TestUSGeneralRulesUnchanged` pins the strings.
- `tariffshift.CanadaRules()` loads `rules_ca.json`. No code is copied: lookup, the shift test per alternative, de minimis and the essential-character step are shared.

## D722 — How SOR/94-23 differs from 19 CFR 102, and what the check does with each (22 Nov, #663)
Read from SOR/94-23 ss. 2 to 13 against 19 CFR 102.1 to 102.19 (eCFR, 18 Nov 2026).
- **Same subheading counts (s. 12(2), Schedule III).** 102 Canadian alternatives (88 of them encoded) allow "a change ... from any other good of that subheading" (or heading). Parts rows show it most: 8414.90 is "from any other good of that subheading or any other heading" in Canada, "from any other heading" in 102.20. The check counts a material in the good's own subheading (or heading) as a shift. Reading: a material incorporated into a good is another good; s. 13 (non-qualifying operations) is carried as an assumption, as 102.17 is.
- **Textiles are in the table.** 102.11 sends textiles to 102.21, which is not encoded; Canada has no separate textile rule, so chapters 50 to 63 are ordinary rows.
- **De minimis by weight for chapters 50 to 63 (s. 11(1)(a)).** The check reads `weight_share` there; value is not used. Elsewhere 7% of value, 10% in chapter 22, as 102.13.
- **De minimis excludes chapter 6 too (s. 11(1)(b)).** Canada: chapters 1 to 4, 6 to 8, 11, 12, 15, 17, 20. 102.13(b) has no chapter 6.
- **Origin by a chapter note (s. 4(1)(d)).** See D723.
- **Production in another CUSMA country (s. 9).** An answer of Canada for a good produced in the United States or Mexico becomes that country, assuming the work there is more than minor processing. 102.19(b) was the U.S. counterpart and applies only to goods entered before 1 Jul 2020.
- **Tariff preference override (s. 8) still in force.** Where the answer is not a single CUSMA country, a CUSMA-originating good with a certificate of origin takes the last CUSMA country of production. 102.19(a) lapsed on 1 Jul 2020. The check cannot see a certificate, so it does not apply s. 8; a decided answer that is not a CUSMA country says so in its assumptions.
- **Non-qualifying operations (s. 13)** have no "simple packing, repacking or retail packaging" (102.17(c)); minor processing (s. 2) has no "putting up in measured doses, packing, repacking" (102.1(n)(6)). Only the assumption text changes; neither is decided by code in either set.
- **Disregarded materials (s. 12(1))** have no retail packaging classified with the good (102.15(a)(1)). The input has no packaging field, so nothing changes in code.
- **Essential character (s. 2(2), s. 5).** Same test as 102.18(b)(1) and 102.11(b); Canada names materials of the same tariff provision and self-produced materials explicitly. s. 2(2) has no counterpart of 102.18(b)(1)(iii) (one material is the essential character); the check reads a single candidate the same way, as the only material s. 2(2)(a) lets it consider.
- **Scope (s. 3(1)).** The rules apply to goods imported from a CUSMA country; every decided answer carries that assumption. Which goods must be marked (Schedule I) is not checked.
- **Codes.** The rows use Canada's tariff at the HS level the regulation was last amended to (2019 tariff, HS 2017). Codes match U.S. codes to six digits except where the HS changed since.

## D723 — Notes that set origin by a process (22 Nov, #663)
57 rows carry one of these notes. Section II (a plant grown in a country is of that country), Section VI notes 1 to 3 (chemical reaction, purification of 80% of impurities, isomer separation), chapter 27 notes 1 and 2 (chemical reaction; distillation for 27.10), and chapter 63 notes 1 and 2 (63.09 and worn-out 63.10: where last collected and packaged) can give the origin whatever the tariff shift says. The codes cannot show those processes. So on those rows a decided answer assumes the note does not apply, and a good whose materials do not shift stays undetermined ("a chapter note gives its own origin test"), never sent to s. 5 by code. Definition notes (fry, substantial assembly, major garment parts, formed uppers, Section VI note 4) are attached as text only.

## D724 — Parity with the U.S. check where the rows are the same (22 Nov, #663)
116 U.S. rows cover the same codes with the same text as a Canadian row, reading "subheadings" as "subheading" (Canada writes the plural for ranges). `TestParityOnIdenticalRows` runs both rule sets on 2,094 inputs built from those rows (the good at the row's first code; one Chinese material at a time from the row's own codes, its exceptions and sources, a code in the good's heading and two far codes; simple assembly, GRI 2(a) and bending unknown, true and false; production in Mexico, no values). Status, origin, each material's answer and the if-not-de-minimis origin agree on all 2,094 (1,029 decided). Production in Mexico and Chinese materials keep s. 8 and s. 9 out; no value keeps de minimis open in both. Only citations and assumptions differ.

## D725 — Shown as a rules check only, with no accuracy figure (22 Nov, #663)
The day-0 check for #663 found about 11 origin and 3 marking rulings in CBSA's published set, none negative, and CBSA's terms need written permission for commercial reuse. That is too few to test against, so no accuracy figure exists and none is shown. Every answer, on the API, the MCP tool and the case page, carries the label "Rules check only — no accuracy figure yet (no published rulings to test against)". Served as `POST /v1/rules/canada-marking` and the `check_canada_marking` MCP tool (on with `RULE_CHECK`, the default). Canada is registered in the market registry of D680 as a rules-only authority (`httpapi.CanadaAuthority`, on with `RULE_CHECK`): a case for Canada gets the SOR/94-23 answer from its product codes as its prediction, with no model call, confidence 0 and fast path 0, so it always goes to review; without codes it has no origin and says what to add. Its origin page shows the check (run on load) instead of the U.S. answer screen. On a U.S. case, the origin page shows a "Check Canada rules" button when the product gives codes for the good and a part. Follow-up steps (plan, letter, broker review) stay U.S.-only, as D680 set for every non-U.S. market.

## D710 — Japan Customs advance rulings on origin: corpus, frozen dev and held-out split, label limits; pre-registration (22 Nov, #661, J3 phase 1)
Committed and pushed before any ruling's detail page was parsed, so before any reasoning, criterion or answer was read. The split uses only the issue date and the agreement (特恵種別) shown on the published search list.
- **Source.** Japan Customs advance rulings on origin (事前教示回答事例（原産地関係）), search at customs.go.jp/searchao, one HTML page per ruling. Snapshot of 22 Nov 2026: the search for every tariff number 01–97 returned 3,606 rulings, issued 2022 (1), 2023 (264), 2024 (1,274), 2025 (1,434), 2026 to 20 Nov (633). Content is under the Public Data License 1.0 (PDL1.0, compatible with CC BY 4.0); attribution and the "edited by" notice are in `data/jp/LICENSE-SOURCE.md`. Built: crawl and parse (`eval/jp/crawl.py`, `eval/jp/parse.py`).
- **Split rule (frozen now).** Held-out: every ruling issued on or after 2026-01-01 (633 on the list). Development: every ruling issued before 2026-01-01 (2,973). Development baseline subset (`dev_eval`): 400 rulings drawn from the development rulings issued in 2025, stratified by agreement in proportion to the 2025 counts (largest-remainder rounding, at least 1 per agreement with any 2025 ruling), seeded random draw (Python `random.Random(20261122)` over ids sorted ascending, per agreement in code order). Written by `eval/jp/split.py` to `data/jp/splits.json`; `--check` rebuilds it from `data/jp/rulings.jsonl` and fails on any difference. A date split mirrors the U.S. held-out windows: the held-out rulings are later than everything the engine is tuned on.
- **Precedent pool.** A case may cite only rulings issued strictly before it. Development runs search development rulings only. Held-out runs (phase 2) search every ruling issued before the case, development and earlier held-out, as the U.S. held-out runs do.
- **Labels.** From the published Japanese fields, never from a translation: agreement (特恵種別), answer (回答), the origin country the answer names (RCEP "原産国", GSP "原産地", bilateral "…原産品"), and the criterion the reasoning (認定理由) relies on, by fixed patterns: wholly obtained (WO), produced only from originating materials (PE), change of chapter / heading / subheading (CC / CTH / CTSH), value content (RVC), specific process (SP). The patterns are written and checked on development rulings only (`eval/jp/labels.py`); it writes held-out labels only when phase 2 scores, and refuses to print them before then.
- **Label limitation, stated now.** On the list every published answer says the good is originating or names its origin; no negative ruling is published (Japan Customs may withhold a ruling up to 180 days; whether negatives are issued and not published is unknown). So no real-ruling figure can measure whether the engine refuses a good that does not qualify. What is measured: (a) criterion match, the engine's deciding criterion against the one the reasoning cites; (b) stated-origin match, where the answer names a country; (c) the share of cases the engine calls originating, which is recall on positives only. Synthetic negatives (one input's tariff number changed so the cited rule fails) may be built in phase 2; they are scored and reported separately and never pooled with or reported as real-ruling accuracy.
- **Phase 1 scope.** Development only: a baseline of the general prompt adapted to "Japan, preference under <agreement>" with BM25 precedents from the development pool, scored on `dev_eval` (criterion match with a Wilson interval, cost, latency). No held-out ruling is scored in phase 1. Phase 2 (engine registered in the jurisdiction registry, then held-out) is pre-registered separately before it runs, and each engine candidate is scored on the held-out split at most once.

## D711 — Japan Customs origin rulings: snapshot, translation, BM25 index and a development baseline, 370 of 400 criterion matches (22 Nov, #661, results of D710)
- **Correction to D710's first line.** Before D710 was pushed (cc617a3a, 20:02 +08:00), one detail page had been read while probing the site: the example ruling 1231386 (issued 2023, a development ruling). No held-out page was read before the split was frozen, and none has been read since: the label patterns were written on development rulings only.
- **Snapshot (built).** 3,606 rulings, the same count the search reported; every page fetched once and parsed with no failures (`data/jp/rulings.jsonl`; `data/jp/snapshot.json` keeps each page's URL, SHA-256 and size, and the fetch window: detail pages 12:01 to 13:10 UTC on 22 Nov 2026, the final list pass from 12:10 UTC). Crawl etiquette: robots.txt allows all paths and was checked first; a plain client name (`rulings-research-crawler/1.0`); request starts at least 1.1 s apart, at most three connections; resumable. The site's own result label is wrong on the last page ("3601～1000"), so the crawler counts rows instead. Raw HTML (about 55 MB) is not committed. Licence: PDL1.0; attribution and the edit notice in `data/jp/LICENSE-SOURCE.md`, licence text in `data/jp/LICENSE-PDL1.0.ja.txt`, entry in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.
- **Counts.** By issue year: 2022 1, 2023 264, 2024 1,274, 2025 1,434, 2026 633 (to 6 Nov). By agreement: Japan-EU EPA 1,305, CPTPP 670, AJCEP 633, RCEP 402, Japan-US TA 234, GSP 168, Japan-India 42, Japan-Thailand 35, Japan-Indonesia 29, Japan-Australia 28, Japan-UK 28, Japan-Vietnam 14, Japan-Malaysia 6, non-preferential 6, Japan-Mexico 2, Japan-Philippines 2, Japan-Switzerland 1, Japan-Chile 1. 65 tariff chapters; most: 64 footwear 570, 62 woven apparel 379, 02 meat 236, 44 wood 215, 35 proteins and glues 206, 24 tobacco 179, 61 knitted apparel 154, 39 plastics 152; chapters 84, 85, 87 and 90 together 4. `eval/jp/index-stats.json` (`go run ./cmd/jpeval index`).
- **Split (D710 rule, frozen).** Development 2,973, held-out 633 (Japan-EU 234, RCEP 98, Japan-US 85, CPTPP 75, AJCEP 60, GSP 37, Japan-India 18, Japan-Australia 10, others 16), `dev_eval` 400 (Japan-EU 181, CPTPP 85, AJCEP 56, RCEP 31, Japan-US 22, GSP 7, 12 other agreements 18). `data/jp/splits.json`; `eval/jp/split.py --check`.
- **Labels (development only).** All 2,973 development answers are positive. Criterion, from the rule the reasoning says is met: CC 1,154, CTH 1,097, CTSH 334, SP 261, WO 121, PE 3, RVC 3; 2,226 answers name a country or the EU. Value tests are rare in these rulings: 16 more cite a value test beside a change of classification (`criteria` keeps both). Two pattern changes were made after reading development errors from the baseline below, and are disclosed: (1) a quoted product-specific rule that certain materials be wholly obtained (Japan-EU cheese, flour) is SP, not WO; this moved 65 development rulings from WO to SP, 15 of them in `dev_eval`; (2) the SP definition is now "any other product-specific rule" (a process, or a wholly-obtained-materials condition). The builder read the quoted rule of 40 random development rulings against their labels; all 40 agreed. That is a builder check, not a review by a Japanese customs specialist.
- **Translation (built).** Every ruling's product, materials, process, reasoning, legal basis and answer translated by gemini-3.8-flash through an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM gateway to Gemini (`jp-translate-v1`, temperature 0), Japanese kept alongside in `rulings.jsonl`. $6.98 for 3,606 rulings (about $0.0019 each; p50 4.4 s, p95 6.4 s), plus a $0.05 pilot on 21 rulings. Mechanical check on the 2,973 development rulings (`eval/jp/check_translations.py`, `eval/jp/translation-check.json`): every tariff and chapter number kept in all 2,973; quoted rule codes kept in 2,969 (4 translated "CTH" into words); the named origin country kept in 1,155 of 1,155. The builder also read 8 development translations against the Japanese: all faithful. Translations are for search and reading; no label comes from them.
- **Retrieval (built).** `internal/jpcorpus`: BM25 over the English case facts (product, tariff number, agreement, materials, process; never reasoning or answer) with the U.S. index's tokens and settings, and the U.S. strictly-earlier precedent filter (ids prefixed `JP`). A precedent's holding is the English answer plus the end of its reasoning, where the rule met is named (900 characters). Label-free check: the top precedent claims the same agreement as the case for 354 of 400 `dev_eval` cases (88.5%).
- **Development baseline (measured, development set only).** `go run ./cmd/jpeval baseline -split dev_eval -tag d711` at 7395853b (RUNLOG `jp-dev_eval-gemini-4-argon-jp-baseline-v1-litellm-d711`, 21:28 +08:00): engine-v1's general prompt adapted to "Japan, preference under <agreement>" (`jp-baseline-v1`, eval only), gemini-4-argon, 5 BM25 precedents from development rulings issued before the case. **Criterion match 370 of 400 = 92.5% (95% CI 89.5–94.7)** with the labels as now committed; 368 (92.0%, 88.9–94.3) with the labels before the two pattern changes. Majority baseline (always CC, the commonest criterion outside `dev_eval`): 144 of 400 = 36.0%. Says originating 396 of 400 (recall on positives only). Origin named by Japan Customs (not EU): 110 of 111. By agreement: AJCEP 55/56, CPTPP 82/85, Japan-EU 162/181, Japan-US 21/22, RCEP 27/31, the rest 23/25. No call failed. $2.93 ($0.0073 a case; 2,634 input and 222 output tokens a case), p50 6.7 s, p95 11.1 s. `eval/jp/baseline-dev-metrics.json` (`go run ./cmd/jpeval summary -check`). A 5-case format check ran first ($0.04, tag `smoke`, not scored for anything).
- **Where it misses (development rows).** 30 misses: 12 SP rules (10 called CC: 8 Japan-EU cheeses, wheat flour and potato flakes, whose rule is that the chapter 4, 10 or 11 materials be wholly obtained; 1 called PE, 1 WO); 11 change-of-classification level errors (CC, CTH and CTSH confused); 4 answered "does not qualify" (a distilled spirit, particleboard, a skewer set, modified starch); WO called PE twice (RCEP dried fruit); one value rule (mirin, RVC40 and CTH) called CTH. The engine was less sure on misses (mean stated confidence 0.91 against 0.99 on matches).
- **Not done (phase 2).** No held-out ruling scored. Needed: a Japan engine registered for `jp` in the market registry (D680, now on main) that uses `jpcorpus` retrieval and a prompt whose SP definition covers wholly-obtained-materials rules; product-specific rule text per agreement (RCEP's Annex 3A is on main, D690, and D691 pre-registers its own check on these rulings; the other agreements are not encoded); held-out labels written with `labels.py --held-out --confirm-phase2`; a pre-registration naming the engine, the held-out precedent pool (every ruling issued before the case) and the synthetic-negative protocol, pushed before the single held-out run; review by a Japanese licensed customs specialist before any coverage claim.
- **Spend:** $10.00 gateway-reported (translation $7.03, baseline $2.97). Programme total after this: $122.95 of the $500 cap.

## D712 — Japan trade-agreement candidate and one-time scoring protocol (23 Nov, #682)

- **Candidate.** Freeze `jp-engine-v1` with `gemini-4-argon` on an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM gateway to Gemini. It receives the stated agreement, finished-good tariff code, manufacturing facts and applicable rule text. It searches up to five earlier Japan Customs rulings under the same agreement. The code treats a product-specific requirement for wholly obtained materials as SP and distinguishes it from a wholly obtained finished good. Missing inputs, rule text or agreement coverage can yield an undetermined result. Every product result requires specialist review.
- **Rule sources.** RCEP Annex 3A in HS 2022, Japan–EU EPA Annex 3-B in HS 2017, CPTPP Annexes 3-D and 4-A in HS 2012, and AJCEP Annex 2 in HS 2017 for the dates in the source table. The lookup does not transpose codes. It withholds rows that depend on omitted supplemental provisions. The [rule-source record](../backend/internal/jprules/README.md) lists editions and known omissions.
- **Development.** Use the frozen D710 `dev_eval` sample. Development and synthetic runs may retrieve only development rulings. The phase-one 92.5% result remains the original unrestricted development baseline. The new candidate can abstain when it lacks rule evidence, so the baseline and candidate are reported separately.
- **Unseen test set.** Score `held_out` exactly once after this decision and the candidate code are pushed. Use every D710 frozen test row. Generate the labels with the existing Japanese-text extractor after the push. Retrieval may use development and earlier test rulings published strictly before the case date, never the case itself. The model receives facts without the test ruling's reasoning or outcome. Do not retry model calls in this evaluation. An error or abstention stays in the denominator whenever the corresponding label is present.
- **Measures.** Report exact criterion agreement, criterion agreement with any cited criterion, named-origin agreement (including a separate country-only number), and recall on published affirmative rulings. Report agreement-level denominators, outcomes, model-call failures, Wilson 95% intervals, cost per case and gateway latency p50 and p95. Published affirmative rulings measure how often qualifying goods are recognized. They cannot establish how often ineligible goods are refused.
- **Synthetic negatives.** Score the committed `eval/jp/synthetic-negatives.jsonl` once and separately. The fictional RCEP cases use a central non-originating input in the same heading or chapter as the finished good, above the applicable de minimis allowance, where Annex 3A offers no alternative criterion. Count explicit refusals, abstentions, erroneous positives and failures separately. These cases do not estimate performance on rejected Japan Customs applications.
- **Release.** Keep the Japan authority behind its dedicated gateway settings. Specialist review and production activation belong to the repository owner ([#665](https://github.com/kendramoss/wassup-hackathon-2026/issues/665), [#694](https://github.com/kendramoss/wassup-hackathon-2026/issues/694)).

## D713 — Japan development result and candidate selection (23 Nov, #682)

On the 400 D710 development cases, the candidate matched the cited criterion on 243 (60.75%, Wilson 95% interval 55.88–65.41). It called 244 qualifying, sent 155 to review without a decision, and had one failed call. Among the 244 it called qualifying, 243 matched the cited criterion. It matched 51 of 111 named countries and 177 of 292 named origins including the EU. It had no rule or input to call the model on 51 cases. The original D711 development baseline matched 370 criteria. D712 keeps the lower-coverage candidate as a preliminary assessment because it requires published rule text and can abstain. The full-denominator comparison remains visible. Every result goes to specialist review.

The full development run cost $2.9794, or $0.0074 per row, at p50 6.971 s and p95 10.079 s for rows with a model call. A prior attempt stopped with 17 saved rows, including eight timeouts and $0.0414 in reported charges. The saved partial results and complete run are in `eval/jp/runs/` and `eval/results/RUNLOG.jsonl`. Six workers completed the full run. Use six workers on the one-time held-out run and two on the synthetic batch. No data or prompt changes were selected from held-out results.

## D714 — Japan held-out gateway failure and synthetic fixture date correction (23 Nov, #682)

The D712 candidate was pushed at `ed6c73992677587a227aa8bff4310ce8bf959d00` before held-out labels were generated. The single run processed all 633 positive Japan Customs rows. It made a model request on 382 rows, and the gateway returned HTTP 403 on every one. It abstained before a request on 251 rows: 162 without an embedded agreement schedule, 85 without an applicable HS rule and four non-preferential cases. The run produced no model predictions and no reported charges. Preserve the rows and the mechanical zero match count as an operational failure. The gateway errors prevent an unseen-set accuracy estimate.

The synthetic command's initial validation rejected the fixture dates before opening the run file or sending requests. Set only the dates of the eight existing fixtures to 31 December 2025, before the D710 holdout boundary. The same RCEP HS 2022 schedule applies on this date. The facts, expected refusals and scoring rules stay frozen. Commit and push this amendment before the separate synthetic run. The held-out record stays tied to its original commit and run.

## D715 — Separate synthetic RCEP attempt and release status (23 Nov, #682)

After the D714 date correction was pushed at `bff2b807341970615321bd8b84bbd96bbc95fe75`, the eight fictional cases were sent through LiteLLM once. Each returned HTTP 403. The gateway reported $0 and no refusal assessment came back. Keep the synthetic rows separate from the Japan Customs results. The planned accuracy and refusal measurements remain unavailable. Production activation and customs specialist review remain open in #694 and #665. This change supplies the four embedded schedule scopes listed in D712.

## D716 — RCEP Japan reproduction protocol details (#666, 23 Nov)

D691 is the pre-registration. The bundled Annex 3A HS 2022 table has the same version and contents as D690. Score the maintained engine after the three pre-existing input and rule-lookup fixes (#671 to #673, commit `0de8dcb8`). Those fixes landed before this evaluation. Keep the engine and inputs fixed after the development run.

The input builder reads the parsed material entries and the explicit manufacturing country at the start of the published production field. Tariff codes keep their published precision, and inconsistent material codes stay unknown. A material is originating only when the material entry makes that statement. A country of manufacture does not establish preferential origin. Values, weights, variant choices and production declarations are left unset. Japanese reasoning is used only after input construction to read the frozen criterion label and the tariff scope or rule-row reference. A general Annex 3A citation does not identify a row. Report a prefix-compatibility check for a cited tariff scope separately from exact-row agreement.

Score the frozen development split before recording the held-out split. Mutate the first input the engine counts as non-originating by replacing its tariff code with the finished good's four-digit heading after a tariff-shift yes. This is a synthetic stress test. A missing fact or an incomplete tariff classification may make the result undetermined. Report that outcome separately from an explicit refusal. Wilson intervals use the outcome's stated denominator.

## D717 — RCEP check on the frozen Japan Customs set (#666, 23 Nov)

D716 was pushed at `cd40dacfb35c106c6be3bcc291549ea1ca5da732` before scoring. The bundled rule table is unchanged from D690. All 402 RCEP rulings in the D710 snapshot qualify in the published decision. The check recognized 162 of 304 development positives and 71 of 98 held-out positives. The other rows were undetermined. There were no refusals or input errors. The published case files often omit preferential-origin declarations and the values needed for value-based tests and de minimis.

On held-out tariff-shift cases with enough material-code digits to test the cited change, 71 of 72 qualified. All 71 decisions matched the published criterion. The only criterion disagreement across the two splits was development ruling 1240464. It cites wholly obtained, and the calculator found a change of chapter without a wholly obtained declaration in the parsed inputs. No ruling explicitly named a unique Annex 3A row. For each of the 388 comparable rulings, the separately cited tariff scope and the calculator's row had compatible prefixes. That checks code consistency.

The synthetic mutations changed 233 affirmative tariff-shift outcomes to undetermined. None produced an explicit refusal or stayed yes. Neither test set measures refusal performance on real rulings, and the corpus had no primary RVC labels. Run recordings, Wilson intervals and limits are in [RESULTS](../eval/RESULTS.md#rcep-calculator-on-japan-customs-rulings-d691-d716-d717). The run made no model calls and cost $0.

## D726 — A pending invitation records the admin who sent it; legacy invitations stay anonymous (23 Nov, #712)

An invitation now stores the email of the admin who sent it, beside the invited list. The first sender is kept when another admin invites the same email again, and the record survives that admin leaving or losing the role. Joining consumes the record, so a later invitation is attributed to its own sender. `GET /v1/workspaces/mine` returns it as `invited_by`, which is optional in the API.

An invitation stored before this change has no sender. The API omits `invited_by` for it and the page reads "You were invited to <workspace>." It does not guess the workspace creator. `created_at` stays the time the workspace was created, not the time of the invitation. A legacy invitation that several admins sent stays unknown, because nothing says which came first. This changes no join, cap or authorization rule.

## D727 — Split-group money in the legacy comparison follows the operations first (23 Nov, #716)

Without an operations block, the money path prices a moved group from one baseline plant. That plant is the plant of the group's operations when it has any, otherwise of its components. Several plants at that tier mean there is no single baseline, so added cost and net are unknown rather than picked from list order. An operation at one plant with a component at another is not split, which keeps the earlier BOM golden unchanged. The operating-cost mode keeps its own, broader definition and is not changed here.

A variant that consolidates a split group changes the group's plant set even when the legacy move list is empty, because the first-listed operation can happen to match the variant. The legacy path now treats a current group with several money plants and a changed plant set as unknown money, in either operation order. A reordered but otherwise unchanged split group is not a money move. A group that is single-plant today, including one the variant splits partly, is priced as before. Legal enumeration, the move list, `MatchMove` and the legal checks still use the first-listed plant, so which candidates the search tries is unchanged. Duty savings stay known. With no group costs entered, the comparison remains duty-only.

## D728 — Duty pricing identifies a country by one name; the money forms keep one rate per country (23 Nov, #718)

Duty pricing reads a country through `DutyCountry`, which is `NormalizeCountry` plus a short list of verified spellings, for example "Chinese Taipei" for Taiwan, "UAE", "Korea, South" and "S. Korea" for South Korea. It is not a world country list. `NormalizeCountry` and the origin facts built on it are unchanged, so "S. Korea" still normalises to "S Korea" there. The TypeScript copy in `frontend/src/lib/duty-rates.ts` is checked against the same fixture, `backend/internal/domain/testdata/duty_country.json`, whose expectations are the duty identity.

When saved rates hold several spellings of one country, the backend uses the exact canonical name, otherwise the first key in sorted order. That is a fallback for rates that arrive over the API, since two explicit rates do not show which one the user typed. The money forms never write duplicates. Editing a rate collapses every spelling of that country to one entry under the plant's own spelling and drops that country's auto-fill origin marks, because the rate is now the user's. The forms show a note when saved rates contain such duplicates. Country names in the helper's lookup tables are free text, so they are read as own properties only.

## D729 — Verifier repair slots carry the enforced-edge fingerprint (23 Nov, #721)

A verdict that replaces an unusable stored one is written to `<key>-val2-<fingerprint16>`, where the fingerprint covers the supersession edges this instance enforces (the earliest edge per ruling that `SupersededAsOf` reads). Earlier builds wrote `<key>-val2`; that slot is still read, through the same checks as the other slots, so existing repairs are not discarded. A changed edge opens a new slot because the stores never overwrite a key. This supersedes the slot name in D111 and does not change `ValidationEpoch`.

Cost: any change to the enforced edges, even for an unrelated ruling, moves the fingerprint. A task whose current repair slot is empty and whose older repair was written under a different fingerprint is verified again once, which is a paid model call for that task. This is bounded to tasks already in repair slots, because verdicts under the base key and the legacy slot are not invalidated. Nothing here claims cross-instance or production behaviour.

## D730 — Production activation of the audit trail, required sign-in and bearer check (#561, 23 Nov 2026)
- **Why:** D290 recorded these three controls as built and tested but "not switched on" on undelabs.dev. #561 asked for the owner/infrastructure step. No code change was needed: the flags, the frontend proxy's bearer forwarding and the tests already existed.
- **Decision:** turn all three on in **three separate deploys**, verifying each before the next, rather than flipping them together. The public demo opens through the pinned demo cases and `/v1/demos*`; no demo account was created. Code defaults stay permissive for local work.
- **Alternatives:** flipping all three at once was rejected because Cloud Run's bearer pass-through to the container had never been measured; leaving them off was rejected by the owner.
- **What was done (all on `main`, each merged through a PR and deployed with a manual `workflow_dispatch`, because a `deploy.yml`-only merge does not pass the `changes` filter):**
  1. `audit-actor-key` v1 created in Secret Manager; `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` granted to `agent-backend@wassup-hackathon-2026.iam.gserviceaccount.com` (the first deploy failed without it); wired as `AUDIT_ACTOR_KEY` with `AUDIT=auto` (PR #739, deploy run `45133247856`, revision `backend-00194`). Verified `/api/v1/audit` and `/api/v1/audit/verify` went from 404 to 403/401, i.e. registered.
  2. `STRICT_AUTH=on` (PR #741, deploy `45135033124`, revision `backend-00196`). Verified `GET /api/v1/cases` anonymous → 401, `GET /api/v1/demos` → 200, an invalid `Authorization: Bearer` → 401 on a private route (no anonymous fallback), homepage → 200.
  3. `REQUIRE_BEARER=on` (PR #742, deploy `45137349712`, revision `backend-00197`). Verified `GET /api/v1/demos` still → 200 with the flag on, which proves Cloud Run forwards the frontend's header to the container; `GET /api/v1/cases` → 401, direct backend `/health` → 403 from Google Frontend, no `allUsers` in the backend IAM policy. No rollback was needed.
- **Evidence recorded:** live `curl` status codes above; `STRICT_AUTH=on` and `REQUIRE_BEARER=on` present in the deployed Cloud Run env with `AUDIT_ACTOR_KEY` bound to the secret; no `production config` startup warning in Cloud Logging for the new revision; CI green (`changes`, `backend`, `frontend`, `ci-ok`) on all three PRs. The annotations about a missing `before` field and five pre-existing unused-symbol lint warnings are informational.
- **Limits:** an interactive Google OAuth click-through was not run here — the verification-path checks (invalid token → 401, public routes still 200) are the evidence for sign-in. The audit trail is evidence, not a certification or an immutable log; head export, external anchoring and a retention/TTL policy remain planned (audit-trail.md section 8). Nothing here changes the Japan coverage wording or any accuracy claim.

## D731 — Live sign-in blocks the second anonymous ADK run (23 Nov, #683)

- **Pre-registration.** D510 requires each session to create a new anonymous case over the live MCP endpoint. Run 1 is the historical result in D511. The daily model budget had reset when we checked the second run.
- **Observed.** Since D730, live case creation requires sign-in or an API key. The anonymous MCP client initialized and listed tools. An intentionally invalid-date `predict_origin` probe then returned HTTP 401 `unauthenticated` before input validation. The probe could not create a case or reach a model. The sanitized response is in `eval/agent/adk/live-v2-run2-preflight.json`.
- **Decision.** Stop before starting the 12 product sessions. Keep run 1 and the D510 scoring rules. Repeatability is unmeasured. An authenticated evaluation would need its own protocol because it would change how cases are created and accessed.

## D732 — Pre-registration for an authenticated live ADK evaluation (#683, 23 Nov 2026)

- **Question.** How reliably does the D510 agent complete its workflow for a signed-in API caller? D731 blocked anonymous run 2. This is one separate authenticated run per product and cannot measure the original anonymous protocol's repeatability.
- **Inputs and configuration.** Freeze a01–a12 from `eval/agent/products.jsonl`, the saved D470 agent instruction and tool filter, Gemini 3.8 Flash through the approved LiteLLM gateway, and live `https://undelabs.dev/mcp`. Start fresh ADK sessions in fixture order in batches of up to three. Make one new private case per session and at most one plan search. A timed-out plan call may rejoin the same search with the original idempotency key, as in D510. Do not rerun a product.
- **Authorization and safety.** Push this decision and the harness before any model run. Obtain an approved secret reference for an evaluator-scoped Unde API key and inject it as `UNDE_API_KEY` only for the eval process. The runner's `--require-bearer` mode sends it as a bearer credential to the live MCP endpoint. Keep it out of model input, tool arguments, logs, and artifacts. Use the production controls and existing quotas. No change to owner settings or authentication. Preregistered and awaiting the scoped key.
- **Checks.** Apply D510's workflow and answer checks, including order, same-case plan and export, plan idempotency, plan selection, one successful draft, supported citations, the disclaimer, and no-plan honesty. Read the no-plan answers by hand and report disagreements. Under D730, the scoped key owns the private case and `predict_origin` returns no `case_access_key`. For bearer rows, require the case ID returned by the prediction on later plan and export calls and require omission of the anonymous case key. Anonymous rows keep their original case-key check and scores.
- **Artifacts and comparison.** Save every started fixture, refused tool call and error in `eval/agent/results/live-v2-authenticated-run1.jsonl`. Its `.meta.json` records D732, bearer auth, the pushed revision, model, endpoint, execution window and `live-v2-run1` as the historical comparison. Leave the original v2 series and both anonymous records intact. Report pass counts out of the 12 scheduled products, unstarted products if any, per-product transitions, tool refusals, gateway spend and duration. Compare descriptively with D511's 9/12 overall and 8/8 on a01–a08. In D511 four sessions were cut short by the anonymous daily budget, and a09 passed after reporting a refused plan call. Mark these rows explicitly. Private-case auth, per-client quota and production changes prevent a controlled repeatability comparison.
- **Spend.** D511 spent `$0.4189` against D510's `$2` gateway cap. This follow-up may spend only the remaining `$1.5811` and must also fit the `$500` program cap. Verify the current ledger and remaining cap before starting and after each batch. Stop before the next batch if costs are unavailable, the forecast would exceed either cap, or access or quota is refused. Attribute live MCP tool model fees separately from gateway agent fees and report only observed amounts.

D32's sentence "Held-out confirmed the dev choice; it was not used to search for the bar" and the "never used to tune thresholds" wording corrected in D260 are not claims about the 0.92 bar's origin. ## D735 — Guidance on an undetermined Canada marking check (24 Nov)
- **Decision.** `POST /v1/rules/canada-marking` and `check_canada_marking` add an optional `guidance` object when the result is undetermined: the yes/no facts that would settle it, the codes or shares to add, and the rule readings only a person can make. Requests do not change: the answers are the existing `simple_assembly`, `gri_2a` and `bending_to_shape` fields.
- **How a fact is chosen.** The evaluator records the facts of every clause it tries, even a clause that cannot change the outcome, so its `needs` lists are not used for facts. A fact is reported only if setting it true or false changes the answer or a foreign material's status when the whole check is run again. Domestic materials count only where the essential-character test reads them. Rules written by goods description (the unencoded alternatives, and the goods-description clauses) are shown as review items, never as a question.
- **Scope.** Marking context under SOR/94-23 only: it is not a Canadian preferential-origin or customs-agency determination, and not a 19 CFR Part 102 or USMCA qualification. `evaluate` output is unchanged (a golden test pins it); `guidance` is not on `tariffshift.Result`, so the case rule check is unchanged.
- **Reach today.** Schedule III as encoded has no simple-assembly, GRI 2(a) or bending clauses, so on the committed Canadian table the guidance holds codes, shares and review items; the fact questions appear when a rule that carries such a clause is loaded. Real today: codes (a missing or too-short code), shares (value or weight, for de minimis) and human review. The yes/no controls are proven on synthetic tables only. The UI supplies shares from typed percents by re-running in `good_hts` + `materials` mode, so a share item is actionable on a product-based check too.

## D740 — USMCA origin-rule check: three pilot rows, exact RVC, own route and MCP tool (24 Nov)
- **Decision.** `POST /v1/usmca/check` and `check_usmca_origin_rule` check one selected USMCA product-specific rule (HTSUS General Note 11(o), Rev 23) for goods entering the United States. Deterministic Go in `backend/internal/usmca`, no model call, nothing stored.
- **Scope.** Pilot goods 8202.31, 8207.13 and 9503.00 only; everything else returns `not_supported`. Answer is `met`, `not_met`, `needs_information` or `not_supported` for the selected rule, with the exact RVC (transaction value or net cost, elected by the caller, never defaulted). Not a certification, tariff rate, duty saving or legal finding of origin; a `not_met` is about the modeled alternatives only.
- **Unmodeled provisions.** Parts route, de minimis, sets, accessories and packing, fungibles, intermediate materials, cost averaging, outside-party operations and special valuation must be confirmed not applicable, and accumulation, remanufactured goods and automotive rules are not evaluated and are covered by the same confirmation; one marked as applying returns `not_supported`. The screen words the one tick as what the user is not relying on, never as "no parts" or "no automotive use". Furniture (9403/9405) is excluded until the HS-edition correlation is verified.
- **UI.** A separate "USMCA origin-rule check" fold for U.S. cases; amounts are sent as strings, the materials list is never assumed complete, and a late response cannot replace the result for newer facts.

## D741 — Japan re-run: public gate, new run ids, call plan, budget guard and a new pre-registration (24 Nov, #694, #735)

This is a prospective pre-registration for a new held_out and synthetic run of candidate `jp-engine-v1` with model `gemini-4-argon` through the LiteLLM gateway. It takes effect at the pushed commit that is later passed as `-prereg`. No scored output of the new run exists when this record is written. It does not activate Japan, and it does not claim a specialist review (#665 closed only because Japan is not available yet).

- **Public gate.** `JAPAN_ENGINE=on|off`, default off, decides whether the Japan authority registers at all. Gateway settings alone never register it, and the local fake provider needs the gate too. Production stays off.
- **What changed since D712.** The `jp-engine-v1` prompt and engine code in `internal/jpengine` are unchanged since the D712 candidate commit. The embedded schedules grew with #738, so the eligible held-out requests rose from 382 to 421 (212 abstain before a request, from 251). The RCEP engine, domain package and corpus tests also changed, and the eight synthetic fixture dates were corrected in D714. The D712 pre-registration therefore no longer matches the tree, and the one-run guard still refuses any drift. This decision is the new pin. The D712 protocol and the D714 and D715 gateway failures stay as recorded. The 403 responses were never explained: the original error text was reduced to a class before saving. A new authentication check is needed before anyone states a cause.
- **Unchanged protocol.** One request per eligible case, no retries, output cap 8192, gateway cache skipped, held_out with six workers and synthetic with two. The denominators stay 633 and 8, with every error and abstention counted. Datasets, labels, prompt, scoring and model settings are not tuned from held-out or synthetic results, and they are not selected or reported selectively. The held_out run goes first, then synthetic. Whatever the outcome, both are reported.
- **Run ids.** The held_out run is `d741-heldout-1` and the synthetic run is `d741-synthetic-1`. The earlier fixed-name run files stay untouched, and a run id never reuses an existing file. The run log refuses a second run of the same split under one decision.
- **Frozen paths.** The freeze covers every package compiled into the command, including the transport, the scorer, the failure classifier and the new budget guard. A test fails when the command starts to depend on a package outside the list. There is no flag that allows drift.
- **Call plan.** `jpeval plan -split <split>` counts the requests offline with a counting fake model and prices no outcome. On this tree: held_out 421 requests, 5,120,763 request bytes (largest 15,671); synthetic 8 requests, 97,480 bytes. Bytes bound input tokens from above, and every request is priced at its full output cap. The plan hashes the request bodies.
- **Budget.** All paid calls share one ledger with a hard cap of $50 in total: admission and smoke checks, synthetic and held_out. Each call reserves its worst case under a file lock before it is sent, so workers and runs cannot pass the cap together. Rates must be verified and named before any paid call. A run whose worst case does not fit what is left is not started. The gateway's cost header is recorded when present. A response without one is priced from its token usage and the verified rates, and a rejection without one is bounded by its input. Neither is shown as free, and a call with neither keeps its full reservation. Saved rows record the provenance, and the run log records the rates and their source. The gateway's promotional pricing is not assumed to be current until the key's price metadata or a quote has been checked.
- **Ledger rules.** `jpeval budget-init` creates the one ledger of the suite offline. It plans the smoke check, held_out and synthetic together (requests, worst case, request hash) and creates nothing if their worst cases do not fit the cap. The first line fixes the cap, model, rates, rates source and that plan. Every later paid command opens that existing ledger and no other: a mistyped or new path never starts another budget, and different values fail closed. Before its first request a phase must match its planned requests, the ledger must not be stopped, and what is left must cover this phase and every phase not yet started. Each phase, smoke included, is then claimed in the ledger (flushed to disk) before its first request, per decision and split, so a crash cannot be followed by a second run under a new run id. Claims are never released. A call settles below its reservation only on a positive reported cost or positive token usage priced at the verified rates. A zero or missing cost without usage, and every error without usage (a 4xx can follow generation), keep the full worst case. If any call settles above its reservation, its real cost is recorded, the ledger halts durably and refuses every later reservation even with room under the cap, and the overspend is reported. Charges already made cannot be undone, and later price changes are a limit of this guard, not a hard-cap claim. A half-written or unreadable ledger is never repaired and blocks all spending. This guards against accidental re-entry, not a hostile file owner.
- **Admission smoke.** `jpeval smoke` sends one tiny request with no case data, a low output cap (64 tokens by default) chosen only for a health check, one attempt and no retry. It writes its own result file, never under `data/` or `eval/`, is part of the ledger's plan and is claimed once. It says nothing about the study, and the study keeps its fixed 8192-token cap.
- **Failure logging.** A failed call saves a closed class and an HTTP status only. Provider text, headers, addresses and keys are never saved or printed.

## D742 — Japan D741 results published (24 Nov, #735, refs #694)

- **Decision.** Publish the completed D741 run as recorded: the two row files and metrics, and two new run records. Nothing in the candidate, prompt, scorer, labels, data or thresholds changed after the results, and no result was used to adjust a gate. D712, D714, D715 and D741 text stays as written.
- **Result.** Held-out criterion match 260 of 633 (41.07%, Wilson 37.31–44.95), positive recall 266 of 633 (42.02%, 38.24–45.90), with 212 abstentions, 363 undetermined and 4 errors inside the 633. Synthetic refusal 8 of 8 (67.56–100). Full detail in `eval/RESULTS.md`, section "Japan D741 re-run".
- **Disclosures.** Positive-only test, not general accuracy or specificity. The precedent pool was chronological and rolling (197 of 863 cited precedents were earlier held-out rulings, none self or future), so the cases were not wholly unseen. The private supervisor stopped after held-out and before any synthetic claim because of a porcelain-status parsing bug; a versioned script ran only the eight untried synthetic cases. Synthetic `code_dirty: true` reflects earlier output files only. Conservative budget charge $4.1258349 of $50, which is not a verified invoice or a future quote. The call used the LiteLLM gateway, not native Vertex.
- **Status.** Japan stays "not available yet" and `jp.supported` stays false. No market-selector activation, no new gateway credential and no professional review (#665 closed on that wording). The figures are an experimental offline measurement, not coverage, and not production activation (#694 stays open until the gateway is configured and approved). D714/D715 are unmeasured gateway failures, not 0% model accuracy.


## D760 — EU and UK non-preferential origin as rules-only checks: sources, versions, licences (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **Question answered.** The non-preferential country of origin of a good imported into the EU or into the UK, from the good's HS code, its materials' codes and origins, and where needed value or weight shares and yes/no facts. Not preferential (trade-agreement) origin, not marking rules, not tariff classification, not a ruling.
- **EU source.** Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/2446, consolidated text CELEX `02015R2446-20261101` (consolidation of 1 Nov 2026, the latest listed on EUR-Lex on 24 Nov 2026), Annex 22-01 and Art. 31-36. EUR-Lex declines to show the 31 MB HTML in the browser view, so the XHTML was fetched from the Publications Office by content negotiation (`http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/02015R2446-20261101`, `Accept: application/xhtml+xml`, `Accept-Language: eng`), retrieved 24 Nov 2026, SHA-256 `87be4f1a432bc0ef35a6c27a94d237a65fc41d036278cf43fd4889a4f79818be`. The Union Customs Code, Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, Art. 59-63, from its latest consolidation, CELEX `02013R0952-20221212`, the same way, SHA-256 `9963c4596d19c9f8f2306ba7e02db475a4da4e3e93b406be2a4e541ca89b237f` (cited, no data taken). Neither file is committed; `go run ./cmd/originrules rules-eu -xhtml <file> -retrieved 2026-11-24` rebuilds `backend/internal/euorigin/rules_eu.json` (version `eu-da2015-2446-annex22-01-v1`).
- **EU licence.** EUR-Lex content may be reused with acknowledgement of the source (Commission Decision 2011/833/EU; EU-owned content is CC BY 4.0 under the Commission legal notice). Consolidated texts are documentation only; only the Official Journal is authentic. The table says so.
- **UK source.** HMRC, *Rules of Origin: Special Rules for Determining Non-Preferential Origin*, version 1.2 dated 12 April 2023, in effect from 10 May 2023, the document SI 2020/1433 reg. 2 refers to (.docx, <https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/643d52d58b86bb0013f1b39b/230320_Non_Preferential_Rules_of_Origin_ORD_FINAL.docx>, from the GOV.UK publication page last updated 10 Sep 2025, where v1.2 is the current non-preferential document), retrieved 24 Nov 2026, SHA-256 `239b6b3d103dd4d22bfc639638759bb41a6ba98233540e150c79b912d22b850d`. `go run ./cmd/originrules rules-uk -docx <file> -retrieved 2026-11-24` rebuilds `backend/internal/ukorigin/rules_uk.json` (version `uk-ord-v1.2-part4-v1`).
- **UK legislation.** The Customs (Origin of Chargeable Goods) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020 (SI 2020/1433) regs 4-11 and Taxation (Cross-border Trade) Act 2018 s. 17 frame the list. legislation.gov.uk answered every automated request for the SI's XML, PDF and Akoma Ntoso with an HTTP 202 bot challenge, which was not bypassed, so the SI could not be hashed. Its regulations were read through an ordinary page fetch of the made version; the code takes no rule data from the SI, only the citations and the framing below.
- **UK licence.** GOV.UK and legislation.gov.uk content is under the Open Government Licence v3.0 "except where otherwise stated"; the reference document states nothing else. The Trade Tariff API licence ambiguity found earlier does not arise: the API is not used (it carries preferential rules only).
- **Not used as ground truth.** EBTI (tariff classification) and the public Binding Origin Information list (outcomes without facts or reasoning). HMRC publishes no Advance Origin Rulings. Neither source has worked examples; the tests use synthetic fixtures, labelled as such.

## D761 — One engine for both lists, not the 19 CFR 102.20 engine (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- Annex 22-01 and Part Four share a shape the tariff-shift engine does not: abbreviated changes (CC, CTH, CTSH, CTHS, CTSHS) with "except from" clauses, rows limited to goods by description ("ex" rows and split headings), process rules ("Manufacture from yarn", "Assembly of semi-conductor products"), a 10% value tolerance, chapter primary rules, and chapter residual rules (major portion of the materials by value or weight; a mixture rule). Bending them into `tariffshift.Rule` would change a package whose U.S. and Canadian answers are pinned. So `backend/internal/nporigin` reads and decides both lists; `euorigin` and `ukorigin` hold each market's table and framing (citations, the general rule, what minimal operations do). It reuses `tariffshift.Digits` and `tariffshift.Range`.
- The tables are built from the official files and keep every row's code, description and rule text verbatim; amendment markers are dropped. A test re-parses each committed row, so the parser and the data cannot drift.

## D762 — How a list row is read and decided (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **Finding the row.** The good's code picks the rows whose code column covers it. One plain row is applied. When the code reaches an "ex" row (only the goods its description names) or split rows, the caller picks the row (`row`), or says `none`; the answer lists the options and never picks one. When the list is by subheading and the good's code has four digits, it asks for six.
- **Change rules.** Only non-originating materials are tested (introductory notes). CC compares chapters, CTH headings, CTSH subheadings; CTHS and CTSHS also accept a change between splits of the good's own heading or subheading, which a code cannot show, so a material in the same heading or subheading is sent to review. "Except from" clauses are encoded with their ranges; an exception named by description ("split heading ex 7228 (a)", "cold-rolled products of heading 7209") sends a material in that range to review; an exception that applies "when this change results from cutting or bending" is a yes/no fact. "Change from headings 7213 to 7215, provided the material has been cold-formed" is its own alternative with a fact.
- **10% tolerance.** Materials that fail a change rule are disregarded when together they are worth no more than 10% of the ex-works price; the value shares are asked for when needed. No chapter of either list sets its own tolerance.
- **Process rules and conditions.** Decided only from a yes/no answer keyed by the alternative ("8473x.2"). Unknown keys are rejected. The chapter primary rules on blanks (chapters 82, 84, 85) are asked only when the row's own rules are not met, because they can then still confer origin (introductory note 2.6).
- **When the primary rule is not met.** If the row's rule names the country of origin itself ("the country in which the animal was fattened ...") or a chapter note does (chapter 2), the answer goes to a person. Otherwise the chapter residual rules apply: the mixture rule when the chapter has one and the good is a mixture (asked); else the country where the major portion of the materials originated, by value or by weight as the chapter says. "Major portion" is read as the largest share by origin; when no origin has more than half, the answer says so. Equal shares, and mixtures some chapters weigh by dry matter, go to a person.
- **Assumptions on every decided answer.** The work is more than minimal operations (Art. 34 DA; UK Part Two), was not done to avoid measures (Art. 33 DA; SI 2020/1433 reg. 4), and no chapter note excludes the change. Accessories, spare parts and tools (Art. 35 DA; Part Three), neutral elements and packing (Art. 36 DA) and wholly obtained goods beyond the rows are not modelled.

## D763 — What each table encodes (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **EU (Annex 22-01, CELEX 02015R2446-20261101).** 37 chapters: 02, 04, 09, 11, 14, 17, 20, 22, 34, 35, 42, 49, 50 to 64, 69, 71, 72, 73, 82, 84, 85, 90, 91 and 94. 446 rows, 542 alternatives. 199 alternatives decided from codes and shares (change, change-from and value rules), 338 process rules decided only from an answer, 5 not read (left to an answer): ex 7205 21 (a) and ex 7205 29 (a) ("CTSH or CTSHS provided recasting or atomizing of the cast alloy": the proviso may govern both changes), ex 7222 (c) and ex 7228 (c) ("CTHS from split heading ex ... (a)"), ex 7226 (d) ("CTHS, except from the same subheading"). By row: 182 decided from codes alone, 259 with a process rule, 5 with an unread rule.
- **UK (Part Four, v1.2).** The same 37 chapters. 452 rows, 552 alternatives: 205 from codes and shares, 342 process, the same 5 not read. By row: 184, 263, 5. The UK has rows the EU does not (8524 flat panel display modules; ex 8525 81, 82, 83 and 89 for the EU's single ex 8525 80; ex 8548 for the EU's ex 8548 90; ex 9021.10 and ex 9021.29).
- **Not covered.** Every heading of the other 60 chapters, and every heading of a listed chapter without a row (in chapter 84 only ex 8443, ex 8473 and ex 8482 have rows). Those goods get `needs_judgement` (D764).
- Pinned by `TestCoverageEU` and `TestCoverageUK`; `go run ./cmd/originrules coverage` prints both, with every unread alternative.

## D764 — Goods without a list rule, and the differences between the EU and the UK text (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **No list rule: a judgement.** The origin of a good the list does not cover is the country of its last substantial, economically justified processing, resulting in a new product or an important stage of manufacture (EU: Art. 60(2) UCC, Art. 32 DA; UK: TCTA 2018 s. 17(3)). That is a judgement on facts no code shows. The check returns `needs_judgement` with the article and never an origin. No model is asked, and the Commission's non-binding guidance for unlisted goods is not used.
- **Minimal operations on an unlisted good.** EU: Art. 34 DA, last paragraph, names the country where the major portion of the materials originated, by weight for chapters 1 to 29 and 31 to 40 and by value for 30 and 41 to 97; with `minimal_operations_only` the check applies it. UK: SI 2020/1433 reg. 9 only says the Part Two operations are not an important stage of manufacture, and reg. 7 covers uneconomic processing, not minimal operations, so the UK check returns a judgement. On a listed good, EU minimal operations go to the chapter residual rules (Art. 34 DA); the UK text does not say, so the UK check returns a judgement there too.
- **"Value of the materials used".** Part Four defines it as the value of non-originating materials, so the UK check decides the three rows that use it (5810, 6307 20, 6307 90). Annex 22-01 has no such definition, so the EU check asks whether the rule is met.

## D765 — Parity where the EU and UK row text is the same (24 Nov, #764, #765)
444 row keys are in both tables. `TestParity` normalises the UK's "Goods Classification Table" to "HS", its spaced codes ("72 28") and spaces before punctuation, and finds 444 rows with the same text. It skips the 3 that turn on the value definition (D764) and runs the other 441 through both checks with four synthetic inputs each (one material from another chapter or from the good's own heading, with every fact answered yes, then no): 1,764 inputs per market, the same status and origin on every one. Citations, assumptions and the framing of goods outside the list differ by design.

## D766 — Shown as rules checks only; EU common rules and national administration (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **No accuracy figure.** No EU or UK origin decisions with their facts are published (the public BOI list gives outcomes only; HMRC publishes no Advance Origin Rulings), so the checks cannot be scored and no figure is shown. Every answer, on the API, the MCP tools and the case page, carries a label: EU "Rules check only — no accuracy figure (no published origin decisions with their facts to test against)", UK "Rules check only — no accuracy figure (no published origin rulings to test against)" (per market since D767).
- **Who applies the rules.** Annex 22-01 and Art. 59-63 UCC are common EU rules. Each Member State's customs authority applies them, issues Binding Origin Information (Art. 33 UCC) and checks declarations; the answer's `administration` field and the EU copy say so. The UK answer says HMRC applies the UK rules and publishes no rulings.
- **Served as** `POST /v1/rules/eu-origin` and `POST /v1/rules/uk-origin`, the `check_eu_origin` and `check_uk_origin` MCP tools (on with `RULE_CHECK`, the default), and the EU and the UK registered in the D680 market registry as rules-only authorities (`httpapi.OriginRulesAuthority`): a case for either market gets the list-rule answer from its product codes as its prediction, with no model call, confidence 0 and fast path 0, so it always goes to review; with no follow-ups, as for every non-U.S. market. Without codes, or with a good the list does not decide, it has no origin and says why.
- **UI.** The origin page of an EU or UK case shows the check, run on load, with the label, the answer, what would decide it (listed, not asked: the question flow is #770) and the rule text, source, version, retrieval date and hash under Details.

## D767 — Review follow-ups to the EU and UK checks (24 Nov, #764, #765)
- **Shares.** The routes refuse value shares, or weight shares, that add up to more than 1 (400): they are shares of one good. Before, 0.9 and 0.95 gave a "decided" answer by the larger.
- **Questions name the fact.** A yes/no need's label now carries the rule's words ("In Taiwan: Assembly of semi-conductor products?"), with the full text as its detail, on the API, the MCP text and the page.
- **HS 2017 rows.** Annex 22-01 rows ex 8525 80 and ex 8548 90 came with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/1063 (marker M3) and were not renumbered when the annex moved to HS 2022, where 8525 80 became 8525 81 to 8525 89 and 8548 90 became 8548 00. Read as written they match no HS 2022 code, so `euorigin` reads them as those HS 2022 subheadings at load. The committed row text and code column stay verbatim. The UK list already has the HS 2022 codes (ex 8525 81 to 89, ex 8548).
- **Per-market label.** The EU publishes Binding Origin Information outcomes, without facts, so the EU label says "no published origin decisions with their facts to test against"; the UK label keeps "no published origin rulings to test against".
- **Northern Ireland.** Under the Windsor Framework the EU's customs rules apply to many goods entering Northern Ireland, so the detector (now `market-detect-v3`) no longer reads Northern Ireland as the UK. A text that names Northern Ireland, Belfast, Londonderry or Derry as the destination gets market `other` with the cue "Northern Ireland", a UK hint and the conflict flag; the case gets no answer and the reason asks the user to pick the market. Work done there is not a destination. No development or held-out ruling text names those places (searched in `backend/data/facts`), so the U.S. figures of D681 cannot change; the probe files were not re-run (one model-written probe, `m2-uk-04`, names Belfast and would now read `other`).
- **Framing tested both ways.** `TestParity` pins 441 rows compared and 3 skipped; `TestFramingDiffers` checks the three cases where the texts differ (minimal operations on an unlisted and on a listed good, and the value rule).
- **Smaller fixes.** No "none of these" option when the rows are splits ending in "Other" (they cover the whole code). A minimal-operations judgement cites its basis. Every decided answer also assumes packing and neutral elements are left out of the materials (Art. 36 DA; SI 2020/1433 regs 5 and 6). The unused wholly-obtained citation was removed. The panel asks its question in one line ("Origin under EU non-preferential rules?") and no longer says "no list rule" on a UK minimal-operations judgement. The market summary says the EU and UK checks cover listed goods only.

## D780 — Tracks 3–6 (#766–#769): case pools and selection rule, written before any count was taken with them (24 Nov)
- **Scope.** Batteries and energy storage (#766), industrial machinery and electromechanical goods (#767), furniture and mixed-material household goods (#768), medical devices and optical or precision instruments (#769). Planner templates, the family check and their tests only; no jurisdiction, API or frontend copy change. No model calls: no budget was granted, so every measurement in D780–D799 is offline and deterministic.
- **What was known before this rule.** An inventory by subject keywords (24 Nov ledger) gave rough counts per family and pool (batteries dev 9 / train 6 / other 11; machinery 22 / 35 / 26; furniture 11 / 22 / 116; medical and optical 4 / 16 / 4). Those counts were seen; no ruling's facts or holding had been read for this work.
- **Universe (`eval/families/depth_b2.py`).** Labelled substantial-transformation rulings with a facts file, dated before 2026, in no `final`, `final2`, `pilot` or `tune_check` list of any split file (including `eval/splits/routed/`), and not among the ruling IDs of `labels_final2.jsonl`, `labels_usmca_final2.jsonl` or `facts_final2` (IDs only are read from those files, to exclude them). Japan data is not used. Pools: **dev** (the development split of `splits_final.json`), **train** (`splits_tune.json` train) and **other** (the rest). Templates cite train and other rulings only, as D660; dev rulings are regression cases and are never cited.
- **Keyword pass.** One fixed pattern per family over the subject and the first 600 characters of the facts (the patterns are in the script and in `b2-hits.json`). A hit is a candidate only.
- **Hand screen (`eval/families/b2-screen.json`).** The agent reads each candidate's subject, facts and holding and keeps it when the good whose origin CBP decides is in the family: batteries — cells, modules, packs, power banks, battery energy storage systems and battery management boards sold as such; machinery — industrial or commercial machines and electromechanical apparatus that do mechanical work (pumps, compressors, motors, machine tools, robots, generators, powered valves and actuators, industrial equipment) and their major subassemblies, not consumer appliances, vehicles or consumer electronics; furniture — seating, tables, desks, cabinets, shelving, beds, mattresses and their structural parts (HTSUS 9401, 9403, 9404 goods), not lamps, bedding textiles or building fittings; medical and optical — medical devices and disposables and optical or precision instruments (lenses, optical assemblies, scopes, microscopes, measuring and diagnostic instruments, eyewear), not drugs, supplements or cosmetics. A screened-out candidate that is another product with a family cue (a tool that contains a battery, a lamp, a drug, a toy with optics) is marked `ambiguous` and becomes a routing test case. Each kept or ambiguous ruling records the reason in one line.
- **Use of counts.** A **new template** is written for a family only if at least 10 kept pool (train + other) rulings are assembled or processed goods of the family not already served by an existing template (D138's bar). Otherwise the work goes into the existing templates' groups and the family check. Each cited ruling is read by the agent and recorded with the holding sentence it rests on (`eval/families/b2-citations.json`); this replaces D138's model citation check, which needs a model call. A group lists rulings where the work was **not enough** wherever the pool has them.
- **Frozen lists.** `b2-cases.json` (from the screen by `depth_b2.py freeze`) is frozen with its date before any template is written from it; changes after that are listed in the decision that makes them.
- **Separation.** Templates carry fact-specific substantial-transformation precedent only. No tariff-shift, regional value content or USMCA/RCEP logic goes into a template or a group note; marking under Part 102 and preference stay in their own engines.

## D783 — A deterministic guard after the family check (`family-guard-v1`) for look-alike products (24 Nov, #766–#769)
- **Problem.** The family check is a model call; its answer is any template or "none". Products that share a cue with a family but are something else — a cordless drill and a battery pack, a floor lamp and furniture, a tablet and a medical device, toy binoculars and an optical instrument — need to go to review, not to a template, and nothing deterministic checked that.
- **Rule.** After the model answers, `familycheck.Guard` reads the product line (the "Typed:", "Product name:" or "Product:" line, else the first line) and the model's product name, takes the head noun (last word before a "for", "with" or comma clause and after the last "of", singular), and takes the match away when one of nine rules fires for the matched family: `battery-material` and `battery-device` (power supplies, chargers and battery packs), `vehicle` (that template and motors/machines), `hand-tool-or-appliance` (motors/machines), `lighting`, `pet-product` and `electrical-cabinet` (furniture), `drug` and `toy` (medical devices; displays, cameras and lenses). It never picks a family, so a wrong rule costs a plan, not a wrong template. The reason names the guard version and rule; the API response shape is unchanged (no new field). `GuardVersion` is bumped with any rule change.
- **Tests.** 44 cases in `guard_test.go`, unsupported and ambiguous products first, each family's own goods kept, and each rule confined to its families; `TestCheckAppliesTheGuard` runs it through `Check`.
- **A fix after the first measurement, disclosed.** The first M2 run (D781) changed 7 of 349 matched development rows; 6 were artifacts: the head noun of a CBP subject ("The country of origin and marking of battery chargers") was read as "country". The head noun now reads after the last "of". The first run's output is kept in the proof directory; the rule set did not change.
